sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
-Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
-Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC → NIPPV → intubation
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion
Put on cardiac monitor

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Character of bleeding: hematemesis? coffee-ground emesis? melena? hematochezia? — hematemesis + hematochezia together indicates a brisk upper GI source
Cirrhosis, portal HTN, varices, prior GI bleed, peptic ulcer disease
NSAID or anticoagulant/antiplatelet use (type, last dose); aspirin
Alcohol use, liver disease
Prior gastric bypass or aortic surgery — aortoenteric fistula risk with aortic graft
Prior endoscopy: any known high-risk lesions?
History of difficult intubation

pairs.value: Nearly 100% specific for upper GI source. Implies active bleeding — most worrisome presentation; urgent EGD needed.
Highly specific for upper GI bleed. Implies less active bleeding than frank hematemesis — blood had time to congeal in the stomach.
Black, tarry stool — strongly suggests upper GI source; can also arise from a slow right-sided colonic bleed.
Bright red blood per rectum — usually lower GI bleed, but ~10% are from a massive upper GI bleed with rapid transit; these patients typically have hemodynamic instability.
Very strongly suggests lower GI source (likelihood ratio ~20 for lower GI).
Collapsed IVC + hyperkinetic LV = volume depletion from hemorrhage. Distended IVC in a shocked patient argues against hemorrhagic shock — reconsider MTP activation.
Suggests cirrhosis. If moderate-to-large ascites present, perform diagnostic paracentesis to rule out SBP and help reduce portal pressure.

Collapsed stomach argues against active upper GI bleeding. Distended stomach in a fasted patient suggests active hemorrhage and increases aspiration risk — consider NG suction before EGD or intubation.

Shock index (HR/SBP) <0.9; full IVC on POCUS; profound anemia with hemodynamic stability (suggests chronic bleed — transfuse slowly, risk of volume overload if given too fast); easily reversible coagulopathy (e.g., supratherapeutic warfarin INR); recent endoscopy without high-risk lesions.

Shock index >0.9; frank hypotension or syncope; normal Hgb with hemodynamic instability (Hgb hasn't fallen yet — implies brisk acute blood loss); active hematemesis; hematemesis + hematochezia together; collapsed IVC on POCUS; known cirrhosis or varices.
Visible vessel = high re-bleed risk. Adherent clot = intermediate. Clean-based ulcer or flat spot = low risk (may discharge or go to ward).
Peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis/gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, varices (esophageal or gastric), portal gastropathy, Dieulafoy lesion, AVM, GAVE, malignancy, aortoenteric fistula, hemobilia.
Age <50: infectious colitis, anorectal disease, IBD. Age >50: diverticulosis, AVM, ischemic colitis, malignancy, post-polypectomy bleed.
AVM (most common >40 yrs), neoplasms (25–40 yrs), Meckel's diverticulum (<25 yrs), Crohn's, NSAID-induced ulcers.
Posterior epistaxis (swallowed blood mimics upper GI bleed, can cause hemorrhagic shock). Bloody diarrhea from ischemic or infectious colitis — bleeding is not the primary problem in these cases.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CBC, BMP, LFTs, INR/PTT/fibrinogen, lactate, type & crossmatch. TEG if cirrhosis or suspected DIC.
-**Access:** Two large-bore IVs (≥18g). Consider RIC or large-bore central access if MTP is running; arterial line if hemodynamically unstable.
-**Monitoring:** Continuous SpO2 + telemetry, frequent BP, strict I&O, Foley.

Resuscitation: Target Hgb >7 (>8 in ACS or hemodynamic instability). Minimize crystalloid — blood products preferred. Give calcium during large transfusions; cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen <150; platelets for count <50. Activate MTP for vasopressor-dependent shock. In cirrhosis/varices: avoid overtransfusion once perfusion is restored — rising venous pressure directly worsens variceal bleeding.

Airway: Avoid intubation unless altered mental status, severe hematemesis, or inability to cooperate with procedure. If intubating: resuscitate first, start vasopressor infusion before induction, assess gastric distension with POCUS, consider NG suction to reduce aspiration risk.

Medications: IV PPI (pantoprazole 40 mg q12h) if upper GI bleed possible. Octreotide (50 mcg bolus → 50 mcg/hr) if varices possible — start empirically. Ceftriaxone 1g IV in definite cirrhosis — evaluate for infection; discontinue within 48–72h if cultures negative. Reverse anticoagulation. Discontinue antihypertensives and DVT prophylaxis.
Prokinetic before EGD or intubation: erythromycin 250 mg IV infused over 5–30 min, ideally 20–90 min before procedure (contraindicated if QT prolonged). Alternative: metoclopramide 10 mg IV.

Source control — Upper GI: Urgent EGD (first-line). Exception: prior aortic surgery → CTA first to evaluate for aortoenteric fistula. Exsanguinating posterior duodenal ulcer with active extravasation on CTA → consider going directly to IR. If EGD fails → IR embolization. Surgery is last resort.

Source control — Lower GI: NG lavage to help clarify source (bloody lavage = upper GI; negative lavage does not exclude upper GI bleed). STAT CTA abdomen/pelvis — only useful while actively bleeding; order immediately if lower GI bleed is suspected. If CTA positive → IR embolization (success rates up to 98%). Avoid tagged RBC scan — poor spatial resolution, unreliable for guiding IR or surgery.

Variceal bleed: Esophageal varices → endoscopic banding; if banding fails → TIPS. Gastric varices → TIPS (preferred); BRTO is an alternative if a gastrorenal shunt is present but is not widely available. Blakemore tube: high-risk, no strong evidence — reserve as a bridge to TIPS in intubated, exsanguinating patients with no other immediate options. Watch for hepatic encephalopathy — low threshold for lactulose and rifaximin.

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.dose: 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr infusion
drugs.notes: Start empirically if varices are possible. Reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal venous pressure. Side effects: dysglycemia, bradycardia, QT prolongation.

drugs.name: Pantoprazole
drugs.notes: Intermittent dosing preferred — continuous IV infusion is not supported by evidence. Continue after endoscopy for peptic ulcer bleed.

drugs.name: Erythromycin
drugs.dose: 250 mg IV over 5–30 min, 20–90 min before EGD or intubation
drugs.notes: Prokinetic — clears gastric contents before procedure; reduces need for repeat endoscopy and aspiration risk during intubation.

drugs.name: Metoclopramide
drugs.notes: Alternative prokinetic to erythromycin when QT is prolonged.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: For patients with cirrhosis and GI bleed. Antibiotics do not clearly reduce mortality. Evaluate carefully for actual infection (SBP, etc.); discontinue within 48–72h if cultures are negative.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.notes: Start before induction if vasopressor-dependent or borderline hypotensive — prevents hemodynamic collapse during intubation.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.notes: Citrate in blood products chelates ionized calcium. Hypocalcemia worsens coagulopathy and cardiac function. Use CaCl 1g if central access available.

pairs.value: Source proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Hematemesis and melena are classic; a brisk upper GI bleed can cause hematochezia.

Portal hypertensive hemorrhage from esophageal or gastric varices. Avoid large-volume resuscitation — rising venous pressure drives the bleeding. Start octreotide immediately and proceed to urgent endoscopy.
Profound anemia + hemodynamic stability = chronic/subacute bleed (transfuse slowly — risk of volume overload). Normal Hgb + hemodynamic instability = brisk acute bleed (Hgb hasn't fallen yet).
Elevated INR reflects rebalanced hemostasis, not a true bleeding tendency. Do NOT give FFP to correct INR. Check fibrinogen; treat with cryoprecipitate if <150 mg/dL. Use TEG to guide transfusion.
Only useful while the patient is actively bleeding — order STAT and don't wait. Preferred over tagged RBC scan, which has poor spatial resolution and cannot reliably guide IR or surgery.

checklist.text: Assess ABCs: active hematemesis or hematochezia with hemodynamic instability = emergent evaluation; call ICU + GI early.
Cardiac monitor and continuous SpO₂.
Large-bore IV access × 2 (≥18g). Minimize crystalloid — blood products preferred for resuscitation.
Type & crossmatch. Activate MTP if vasopressor-dependent or hemodynamically unstable.
Foley catheter for strict I&O — target urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Reverse anticoagulation if on warfarin, DOAC, or antiplatelet therapy.
Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, INR/PTT/fibrinogen, lactate, type & crossmatch. TEG if cirrhosis or suspected DIC.
Characterize bleeding: hematemesis/coffee grounds/melena = upper GI; hematochezia = usually lower GI (but ~10% are brisk upper GI bleeds with rapid transit).
POCUS: IVC (volume status and hemorrhagic shock), gastric distension (aspiration risk), ascites (cirrhosis/SBP).
NG lavage if upper vs lower source is unclear — bloody lavage = upper GI; negative lavage does not exclude upper GI bleed.
IV PPI: pantoprazole 40 mg IV q12h (intermittent dosing — IV infusion adds no proven benefit).
If varices possible: octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus → 50 mcg/hr infusion. Start empirically — do not wait for endoscopic confirmation.
Cirrhosis with GI bleed: ceftriaxone 1g IV — evaluate carefully for infection (especially SBP if ascites present); discontinue within 48–72h if cultures are negative.
Prokinetic before EGD or intubation: erythromycin 250 mg IV 20–90 min before (hold if QTc prolonged — use metoclopramide 10 mg IV instead).
Transfusion target: Hgb >7 (>8 in ACS). Profound anemia with stable hemodynamics = chronic bleed — transfuse slowly to avoid volume overload.
Coagulopathy: cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <150; platelets if count <50; TEG-guided transfusion. Do NOT give FFP to correct INR in cirrhosis.
Upper GI bleed: urgent EGD. Suspected lower GI bleed: STAT CT angiography (only helpful while actively bleeding) → IR embolization if positive.
Monitor CBC, coags, BMP q4–6h while actively bleeding.
GI + surgery consult. IR on standby if endoscopic hemostasis fails.
ICU admission for active GI bleed with hemodynamic instability or airway concerns.
Cirrhosis: low threshold for lactulose + rifaximin — upper GI bleeding is a common precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: **Known liver disease**, cirrhosis, prior decompensation, transplant status
Acetaminophen use, OTC meds, supplements, herbals
Recent drug changes: Abx, antiTB drugs, statins, immunotherapy
Alcohol use history & pattern
Travel history (hepatitis A/E endemic areas)
Autoimmune disease history (SLE, thyroiditis)
Family hx of Wilson's disease or liver failure
!!Pregnancy status!! (HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy)

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Jaundice + coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) + hepatic encephalopathy within 26 weeks of illness in a patient without prior cirrhosis; identify precipitant (acetaminophen, viral, ischemia, Wilson's) — time-sensitive for listing
Hepatic encephalopathy grade (grade I-II at presentation ~40%; grade III-IV ~60% of severe ALF): 1 (confusion/mood): 2 (drowsy/asterixis): 3 (somnolent but arousable): 4 (coma)
Jaundice, scleral icterus
Liver size: tender hepatomegaly (acute hepatitis) vs small/shrunken (fulminant necrosis)
Asterixis (flapping tremor)
Signs of chronic liver disease: spider nevi, palmar erythema, ascites, caput medusae (suggests ACLF, not pure ALF)
Right upper quadrant tenderness
check for cerebral edema: pupillary changes, posturing, Cushing response

pairs.value: MCC in US: intentional OD or unintentional (chronic supratherapeutic use). Check level & start NAC
Hep A, B (most common viral cause), E; rarely CMV, EBV, HSV, VZV
Shock liver: massive transaminase elevation (often >5,000) in setting of hemodynamic compromise
Anti-TB drugs (INH, rifampin), antibiotics, anticonvulsants, statins, herbals/supplements, immunotherapy
ANA, anti-smooth muscle Ab. Steroids controversial: may ↓ survival in highest MELD scores
Young pt, Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, low ceruloplasmin, high urine copper, KF rings on slit-lamp
Budd-Chiari syndrome, hepatic vein thrombosis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
HELLP syndrome, acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP)

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Orders:** IV access x2, Foley (strict I&Os), continuous SpO2, telemetry, neurology consult (if encephalopathy), transplant hepatology consult
-**Stat labs:** LFTs, T/D bili, albumin, INR/PT/PTT, CBC, BMP, ammonia, lactate, ABG, fibrinogen, lipase, blood glucose
-**Etiology workup:** Acetaminophen level, tox screen, hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, HBcAb IgM, HCV RNA, HEV IgM, ANA, anti-smooth muscle Ab, ceruloplasmin, slit-lamp exam (Wilson's)
-**Imaging:** CT abdomen (Budd-Chiari, hepatic vein thrombosis), RUQ ultrasound with Doppler, CXR
-**If bleeding:** Type & crossmatch, TEG/thromboelastometry, fibrinogen, coags
-**Monitoring:** Continuous telemetry, SpO2, q1h glucose checks, q4–6h ammonia, strict I&Os, daily LFTs/INR
ICU referral early: all ALF pts need ICU-level monitoring
Start NAC now if any suspicion for acetaminophen: also improves transplant-free survival in non-acetaminophen ALF
Hold all hepatotoxic medications & unnecessary drugs
Contact transplant center early: ~50% of ALF pts will require transplant (1yr survival 79–84%)
NAC: Start now for acetaminophen & consider for all ALF (improves transplant-free survival in non-acetaminophen causes)
Hemodynamics: Target MAP to maintain CPP 60–80 mmHg. Norepinephrine preferred vasopressor. Balanced fluids over NS. For ACLF: target MAP ≥60 mmHg

RRT / CRRT: CRRT preferred over intermittent HD (↓ cardiovascular instability & cerebral edema risk). Indications: acidbase disturbance, oliguria, volume overload, hyperammonemia independent of AKI. Early CRRT (within 4–12h) for hyperammonemia in ALF improves transplant-free survival. Highvolume hemofiltration (90 mL/kg/h) more effective for ammonia clearance
Infection: Empiric broad spectrum antibiotics if infection signs present. Systemic antifungal prophylaxis for high risk transplant recipients

Transplant evaluation: Urgent for all ALF. Status 1a: ICU + ventilator dependence, RRT, or INR ≥2 with encephalopathy within 8 wks. King's College Criteria better for acetaminophen ALF; MELD more accurate for non-acetaminophen. ACLF grades 1–2: acceptable posttransplant outcomes; ACLF3: careful selection
ACLF3 futility criteria: Age ≥53, lactate ≥4 mmol/L, mechanical vent with P/F ≤200, WBC ≤10 g/L: ≥2 factors predict 8% 1yr survival

pairs.value: ALF-specific: ammonia >200 µmol/L = 55% risk of intracranial HTN. Neuroprotective measures: HOB 30°, avoid fever/hypo/hyperglycemia, maintain Na 140–145 with hypertonic saline, normocapnia, highlevel sedation. Plasma exchange may help. Invasive ICP monitoring NOT routinely suggested

ACLF: lactulose 10–20g q2h until 2 soft BMs, then 2–4x daily. Grade 3–4: give via NG or enema (200g in 700 mL water, retain 30–60 min, q4–6h). PEG 3350 may be superior for rapid resolution. Add rifaximin 550 mg BID (combined > lactulose alone). For ALF: lactulose & rifaximin have NOT demonstrated benefit: focus on treating precipitants, consider plasma exchange

Start vasoactive drugs now when suspected (octreotide 50 µg bolus: 50 µg/h gtt). PPI strongly suggested. High-risk pts (Child-Pugh 10–13 or 8–9 with active bleed): preemptive TIPS improves mortality. If medical + endoscopic therapy fail: TIPS

Vasoconstrictor + albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 2). Terlipressin preferred (response = Cr <1.5 or within 0.3 of baseline, max 14 days). Norepinephrine (0.5–3 mg/h) is noninferior (~50% reversal). Alt: midodrine 5–15 mg q8h + octreotide 100–200 µg q8h (lower efficacy). All AKI pts: urgent transplant eval

Ceftriaxone 2g daily + IV albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 2): albumin ↓ mortality from 41% to 22% at 3 months. Broadspectrum abx within 1h if septic shock. After first episode: secondary ppx with TMP/SMX or ciprofloxacin

Despite ↑ INR, significant bleeding is uncommon (5–7%). INR does NOT predict bleeding risk (rebalanced hemostasis). Do NOT routinely correct with FFP/plts/cryo: may ↑ mortality. Use TEG/thromboelastometry for transfusion guidance. Correction may be needed before high risk procedures (ICP monitoring)

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
drugs.dose: 150 mg/kg IV over 1h, then 50 mg/kg over 4h, then 100 mg/kg over 16h
drugs.notes: Start now for acetaminophen. Also improves transplant-free survival in non-acetaminophen ALF.

drugs.name: Lactulose
drugs.dose: 10–20 g PO/NG q2h until 2 soft BMs, then 2–4x daily
drugs.notes: For ACLF hepatic encephalopathy. Grade 3–4: give via NG or as enema (200g in 700 mL, retain 30–60 min). Not demonstrated beneficial in ALF.

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.notes: Combined with lactulose > lactulose alone for ACLF encephalopathy (↓ hospital stay & mortality). Not demonstrated beneficial in ALF.

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.dose: 50 µg IV bolus, then 50 µg/h gtt
drugs.notes: Variceal hemorrhage: start now when suspected, before endoscopy.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: SBP treatment. Give with IV albumin.

drugs.name: Albumin
drugs.notes: SBP: ↓ mortality from 41% to 22% at 3 months. HRS-AKI: give with vasoconstrictor.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.notes: Preferred vasopressor. Also used for HRS-AKI (~50% reversal rate) when terlipressin unavailable.

drugs.name: Zinc sulfate
drugs.notes: Cofactor in urea cycle: ↓ ammonia in chronic hepatic encephalopathy.

pairs.value: Acute liver failure: coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) + hepatic encephalopathy within <26 weeks of symptom onset in a pt without pre-existing liver disease
Acute-on-chronic liver failure: acute hepatic decompensation in a known cirrhotic with ≥2 organ failures: use CLIFC ACLF score for grading
Encephalopathy within 7 days of jaundice (e.g., acetaminophen, ischemic): best transplant-free survival
Encephalopathy 8–28 days after jaundice
Encephalopathy 29 days–26 weeks after jaundice: worst transplant-free survival

checklist.text: Assess ABCs: hepatic encephalopathy with GCS decline may require intubation for airway protection.
Place on cardiac monitor and continuous SpO₂.
IV access × 2. Fingerstick glucose STAT — hypoglycemia is life-threatening in ALF.
If glucose <60: give D50W IV immediately, then start D10W infusion.
Call hepatology and liver transplant team early — timing of listing is critical.
Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs (AST/ALT/bilirubin), PT/INR (key severity marker), ammonia, acetaminophen level, urine tox, hepatitis panel (A, B, C), autoimmune hepatitis panel, ceruloplasmin, pregnancy test.
Coagulation: INR >1.5 with encephalopathy = diagnostic of ALF — do NOT correct INR unless active bleeding (masks prognostication).
Head CT if encephalopathy present — assess for cerebral edema.
Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler — evaluate liver architecture, Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis.
Acetaminophen toxicity: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) 150 mg/kg IV over 1h, then 50 mg/kg over 4h, then 100 mg/kg over 16h — start even if late presentation.
Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose 20–30 g PO/NG q2–4h titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day. Rifaximin 550 mg PO BID as add-on.
Cerebral edema: hypertonic saline (target Na 145–155), mannitol if signs of herniation, HOB 30°, minimize stimulation.
Coagulopathy: correct only for active bleeding or procedures — use FFP cautiously (can worsen encephalopathy via fluid overload).
Glucose monitoring q1–2h. IV dextrose infusion to maintain >60 mg/dL.
Avoid hepatotoxic medications and nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast if not essential).
Identify and treat precipitant: acetaminophen OD, viral hepatitis, autoimmune, ischemic hepatitis, Budd-Chiari, Wilson disease.
ICU admission. King's College Criteria to assess transplant candidacy.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Atrial fibrillation: #1 risk factor for SMA embolism; check if on anticoagulation
Cardiac hx: recent MI (mural thrombus), cardiomyopathy, prosthetic valves, endocarditis, ventricular aneurysm
Vascular hx: PAD, prior arterial thrombosis, aortic disease
Prior episodes of postprandial pain, food fear (sitophobia), weight loss: suggests chronic mesenteric ischemia (, then acute-on-chronic thrombosis)
Hypercoagulable state: prior DVT/PE, Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, malignancy, OCP use
Recent surgery: esp cardiac bypass (NOMI risk)
ICU pt on vasopressors or with low cardiac output: think NOMI
Anticoagulant use: type, compliance, last dose
Cirrhosis / portal HTN: risk for mesenteric venous thrombosis

pairs.value: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam in a patient with afib, atherosclerosis, or low cardiac output; pain typically periumbilical and colicky early, then constant as bowel infarcts — high mortality with delay
Pain out of proportion to exam (~93%): severe pain with benign-appearing, soft, nontender abdomen early; nausea/vomiting (~75%), diarrhea (~40%)
Tachycardia (often earliest sign); ↓ BP (late: suggests necrosis/sepsis); tachypnea (metabolic acidosis compensation); fever (late)
Soft, minimal tenderness, nondistended: deceptively benign exam despite severe pain
Peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity, rebound) = bowel necrosis has likely already occurred: ominous & late finding
May be hyperactive early: absent late (ileus from necrosis)
Heme-positive stool or frankly bloody ("currant jelly" stools = mucosal sloughing): present in ~25%
Rapid gut emptying (forceful diarrhea) early; AMS, mottled skin, cool extremities if in shock
AFib, recent MI, prosthetic valves, endocarditis, ventricular aneurysm, cardiomyopathy
Atherosclerosis, chronic mesenteric ischemia, PAD, aortic disease/dissection
Hypercoagulable states, malignancy, cirrhosis/portal HTN, pancreatitis, recent surgery, OCP use
Shock (any type), CHF with ↓ CO, vasopressor use, cardiac bypass surgery, hemodialysis, sepsis
Bowel Obst. (SBO/LBO), perforated viscus, pancreatitis, ruptured AAA, volvulus, acute cholecystitis
Aortic dissection with mesenteric malperfusion, renal infarction, splenic infarction
Ischemic colitis (usually less severe, self-limited), C. diff colitis, IBD flare, acute diverticulitis

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CBC, BMP, lactate, LFTs, lipase, coags, blood cultures x2
-Lactate: ↑ as ischemia progresses; nl. lactate does NOT r/o AMI (can be nl. early)
-BMP: AGMA ↑ BUN/Cr (prerenal from dehydration)
-ABG/VBG: base deficit correlates with severity; lactic acidosis
-Ddimer: elevated (sensitive but nonspecific; high negative predictive value)
-Phosphate: hyperphosphatemia (released from ischemic bowel mucosa: relatively specific)
-LDH: ↑ (nonspecific tissue necrosis marker)
-LFTs: AST/ALT may ↑ if portal/hepatic flow affected
-Coags (PT/INR, aPTT): baseline before heparin; DIC screen
-Type & screen: prepare for possible surgery
-BCxs if septic
-**Orders:** IV access x2, NPO, CT angiography (abdomen/pelvis with contrast), vascular surgery consult, continuous SpO2, telemetry
Place on monitor, and get 2 large-bore IV lines.
Call vascular surgery +/- IR early
Keep NPO and begin aggressive IV fluids unless contraindicated.
Start broad-spectrum  ABx .
Start IV heparin unless active bleeding or another clear contraindication.
STAT CTA A/P.
(sensitivity ~94%, specificity ~95%)
Plain Abd XR —nl. early; late: thumbprinting, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, free air

pairs.value: Surgical embolectomy (mainstay) or catheter directed tPA thrombolysis (IR); resect necrotic bowel; second look laparotomy at 24-48 hrs
Angioplasty ± stenting (IR) or surgical bypass/endarterectomy; bowel resection if necrosis
Anticoagulation alone is sufficient in ~95%; catheter directed thrombolysis if worsening; surgery only for peritonitis/necrosis
Transcatheter vasodilator infusion (papaverine) via SMA catheter; txt underlying cause (optimize CO, d/c vasoconstrictors); bowel resection if necrosis
Planned re-exploration at 24-48 hrs: standard after revascularization to recheck bowel viability; don't skip
If peritonitis present: emergent laparotomy for bowel resection; don't delay for further workup

drugs.name: Heparin (UFH)
drugs.dose: 80 units/kg IV bolus (max 5,000 units), then 18 units/kg/hr infusion (max 1,000 units/hr)
drugs.notes: Start now once dx suspected: even if surgery planned, heparinize first. Target aPTT 1.5-2.5× nl. (60-80 sec)

drugs.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
drugs.notes: Covers gram-negatives + anaerobes: bacterial translocation from ischemic gut. Start empirically

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: For critically ill / septic pts or if high resistance risk; alternative to piptazo

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.dose: 25-100 mcg IV q30-60 min PRN; or infusion 25-100 mcg/hr
drugs.notes: For analgesia: do NOT withhold pain control; hemodynamically neutral (preferred over morphine in ↓ BP )

drugs.name: Papaverine (via IR catheter)
drugs.dose: 30-60 mg/hr intraarterial infusion via SMA catheter
drugs.notes: Mesenteric vasodilator: used for arterial embolism & NOMI; administered via IR catheter directly into SMA

drugs.name: !!Norepinephrine!! (if shock)
drugs.dose: 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min IV; use lowest effective dose
drugs.contraindications: Worsens mesenteric ischemia: use only if necessary
drugs.notes: Vasopressors worsen mesenteric perfusion; minimize dose; avoid pure alpha-agonists (phenylephrine)

pairs.value: Inadequate blood flow to intestines: ischemia: infarction: necrosis if untreated; mortality 60-80% overall
Thrombus lodges in SMA (usually at branch points); most common type; classically from AFib or cardiac source
Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing; hx of chronic mesenteric ischemia; highest mortality (70-100%)
Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia: low flow state (shock, CHF, vasopressors) without mechanical Obst.; occurs in critically ill pts
SMV thrombosis: most insidious onset; best prognosis (20-50% mortality); associated with hypercoagulable states
Most common form of intestinal ischemia (80-85%); watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid);self-limited

checklist.text: Recognize the pattern: pain out of proportion to exam, rapid lactic acidosis, or new AFib in an elderly patient — high clinical suspicion.
IV access × 2. Start aggressive IV fluid resuscitation.
NPO immediately. Call surgery and IR (interventional radiology) early — time-sensitive.
Place on cardiac monitor and continuous SpO₂.
Labs: CBC, BMP, lactate (elevated but non-specific), LFTs, coags, type & screen, ABG.
CT angiography abdomen/pelvis (CTA): study of choice — identifies occlusion, non-occlusive ischemia, venous thrombosis; can guide revascularization.
12-lead EKG — new AFib is a risk factor for arterial embolism.
Anticoagulation: IV unfractionated heparin immediately once diagnosis suspected (unless contraindicated by bleeding).
Arterial embolism: endovascular thrombectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis by IR vs surgical embolectomy.
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI): optimize cardiac output, discontinue vasoconstrictors, consider intra-arterial papaverine by IR.
Bowel necrosis or perforation: emergency exploratory laparotomy — surgery consult STAT.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics (gram-negative and anaerobic coverage) if bowel necrosis suspected.
Serial lactate and abdominal exams — clinical deterioration mandates urgent surgical re-evaluation.
ICU admission. Address underlying cardiac cause (AFib rate control, anticoagulation).

sections.title: Can't-Miss Actions
items: !!NPO!! if surgical abdomen suspected
!!Antibiotics early!! if infection suspected (sepsis, perforated viscus, appendicitis)
!!Surgical consultation emergent!! for: peritonitis, perforation, ischemic bowel, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic
Treat the underlying cause — pain control is adjunctive, not definitive

checklist.text: Assess hemodynamic stability: hypotension + abdominal pain = emergency (AAA rupture, perforated viscus, mesenteric ischemia, ectopic pregnancy).
IV access × 2. Cardiac monitor and SpO₂ if unstable.
NPO if surgical emergency possible — do NOT give PO before surgical eval.
Pain management: opioids do NOT mask surgical findings — provide appropriate analgesia.
Focused history: onset, character (colicky vs constant), location, radiation, associated symptoms (fever, vomiting, melena, BRBPR, dysuria), LMP, prior surgeries.
Physical exam: peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding, rigidity) → emergent surgical eval. Pulsatile mass → AAA.
Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, lipase, lactate, UA, urine hCG (all females of childbearing age), blood cultures if febrile.
CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast (preferred) — evaluate for surgical abdomen, obstruction, abscess, ischemia.
RUQ ultrasound if cholecystitis suspected. Pelvic ultrasound if ectopic pregnancy possible.
Early surgery consult for: peritoneal signs, free air on imaging, obstruction, ischemia, or hemodynamic instability.
Monitor serial abdominal exams — worsening exam warrants urgent reassessment.

items: Bilious vomiting in adults = bowel obstruction until proven otherwise

checklist.text: Assess volume status: orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, poor skin turgor — indicate significant dehydration.
IV access. Start IV fluid resuscitation (LR or NS) if unable to tolerate PO.
Check fingerstick glucose — hypoglycemia can cause nausea/vomiting, and prolonged vomiting causes hypoglycemia.
History: onset, duration, associated fever/pain/diarrhea, medications (opioids, antibiotics, chemo, digoxin), recent illness, LMP.
Labs: BMP (hypokalemia, alkalosis from vomiting), glucose, CBC, LFTs, lipase, creatinine, urine hCG if applicable.
KUB or CT abdomen if obstruction, ileus, or surgical cause suspected.
Antiemetics: ondansetron 4–8 mg IV/PO (first-line, minimal sedation); metoclopramide 10 mg IV (also prokinetic); prochlorperazine 5–10 mg IV (second-line).
Correct electrolytes: hypokalemia from vomiting requires IV KCl replacement.
If obstruction: NPO, NG tube decompression, surgery consult.
Treat underlying cause: gastroenteritis, gastroparesis, medication side effect, obstruction, appendicitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis.
Advance to PO liquids once vomiting controlled — clear liquids first, then advance as tolerated.

checklist.text: Active hematemesis: assess airway FIRST — large-volume bleeding can cause aspiration and respiratory failure; intubate early if needed.
Place on cardiac monitor and continuous SpO₂.
Large-bore IV access × 2 (16g or larger). Start volume resuscitation with 1 L LR or NS.
Type & crossmatch. Activate MTP if hemodynamically unstable.
Stat labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags (INR, PTT, fibrinogen), lactate, type & screen.
Assess for varices: stigmata of liver disease (spider angiomata, jaundice, ascites, palmar erythema), alcohol history.
IV PPI: pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr infusion.
If varices suspected: octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus → 50 mcg/hr infusion + ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h.
Urgent GI consult for EGD — target within 12–24h after stabilization (immediately if uncontrolled bleeding).
Reverse anticoagulation if applicable (vitamin K, PCC, or direct reversal agents).
ICU or step-down for hemodynamically unstable or active bleeding.
Serial Hgb q6h while actively bleeding. Transfuse pRBCs for Hgb <7 (or <8 in CAD/hemodynamic instability).
Surgery and IR on standby if endoscopic hemostasis fails.
